['We have had two or three visits from the distinguished Prime Minister of this country, in the last two elections, and before. Once, when my election hung in the balance, the Prime Minister visited the constituency and gave an oration, and I was told immediately afterwards that I need not worry about getting elected. During the next election he came again and made another oration. far more brilliant than the previous one, but as soon as it was over I was assured again that I need have no fear of the consequences. I had a rather peculiar experience in my last election. I had pitted against me a gentleman who to-day occupies a high position in this country as head of the tariff board, a very important position. We got into a very remarkable contest, and while I won the election and he lost, the was able to pull out a $12,000 a year job, while I receive only $4,000. He gave to the world a new epigram, namely, "It is more blessed to lose than to win". I propose to say something about the tariff board before I am through.
I wish to say a word about one of the greatest questions facing this country to-day, and before very long it will take the centre of the platform in this country. I refer to the national debt of Canada. Unfortunately or for tunately, as the case may be, the Dominion of Canada is placed side by side with the great American republic. When we on this side of the line take lightly some of our difficulties, we should cast our eyes across the line and ask ourselves what is this great country to
the south of us doing in regard to some of these matters? Think of this for a moment. In 1919 the national debt of the United States was, in round figures, $25,000,000,000;	1920,
$24,000,000,000;	1921,	$23,000,000,000;	1922,$22,000,000,000;	1923,	$22,000,000,000;	1924,
$21,000,000,000; 1925, $20,000,000,000; and in 1926, $19,000,000,000. In other words, they reduced their debt from $25,000,000,000 to $19,000,000,000 between 1919 and 1926.
But that is not the whole story. Their debt now is reduced almost to $16,000,000,000, I understand, but whatever it may be, we must remember that the United States has placed' on England, $4,700,000,000, upon France almost $3,000,000,000, and under the Dawes report she has placed on the countries in Europe an amount of her debt equal to $11,000,000.000. Take that $11,000,000,000 from the $16,000,000,000, and only $5,000,000,000 remains as the national debt resting upon the United States, and that is being reduced at the^ rate of $1,000,000,000 a year. How are we going to stand five or six years from now. if we have not in the meantime been reducing our national debt by some systematic method; when we are placed in competition with a country right at our doors that has absolutely-wiped out her national debt or has placed it upon other countries? What would be the use of a five or ten per cent tariff then? I claim that one of the most important things for this Dominion to do at this moment is to consider seriously the question of reducing our national debt. We have no country upon which we can unload a single dollar. We must pay off our debt solely through our energy and the genius of our men and the wealth of our resources. When this question of the national debt came up in the budget the Finance minister undertook to pass over it by quoting from an author who has been dead for seventy or eighty years. I marvel at times how the governing body in this country undertake to fortify some of their fallacies by delving into the museums of our country, dragging forth authorities of 150 or 200 years ago, and quoting them for present-day directions. The thing is absurd. Just to illustrate my meaning, I was curious to know who this McCulloch was whom the Finance minister quoted the other day, and I find that he has been dead pretty nearly a hundred years. And I observe, too, that the Finance minister did not read all that he said about national debts. The Finance minister quoted him as saying there should be no sinking fund and no taking care of the debt, but I read the next paragraph to that, just to show you the difference in the minds of men to-day as compared with the minds of men who lived one or two hundred years ago. He says:
The Budget-Mr. Kaiser', 'We have previously endeavoured to show that it would be advantageous to maintain during peace a surplus revenue of some two, three, or five millions a year. We should do this, not so much in the view of reducing the debt, though that is a consideration not to be left entirely out of view, as of increasing our security, and enabling proper measures to be devised, in the event of our being engaged in war, for defraying its expense.
This philosopher said that the great thing for the British Empire to do before it got rid of the national debt was to lay by some ready cash in order to prepare for the next war. Why did not the Minister of Finance explain the mentality of the man whom he quoted in regard to the treatment of our national debt? This man seemed to think he could look down through generations to come and tell exactly what was going to happen, and advise us how we should handle our national debt. But listen to the views of this philosopher on the development of democracy. I wonder what those who are behind the "flapper votes" m England think of this great philosopher's views on the franchise as it should obtain in England. Let me quote:
In a political point of view the late events in America are pregnant with instruction. The system of low or universal suffrage, of allowing the representatives of the nation to be chosen by a numerical majority, including the lowest classes, could not have been anywhere tried under such favourable circumstances as in the United States, and yet the result has been most deplorable. It lias made the mob paramount, thrown the government into the most incompetent hands, and filled the whole country with jobbing and abuses of all sorts. Many of those best acquainted with the people think the crisis will terminate in a military despotism. But whether that be so or not, the experience of the United States is a warning to all nations to beware how they reduce the elective franchise. The Americans are neither better nor worse than others, and the abuses by which they are disgraced would be quite as rampant on this side of the Atlantic were the members of our legislature elected under a similar system.
That indicates the kind of mind that existed fifty years ago. And yet this philosopher is being quoted to-day by the Minister of Finance as a guide in dealing with the national debt!
Now, I consider it important to bring to the attention of the house the strange workings of this strange aggregate known as the "tariff board." They investigated the salt belt, starting somewhere near Kincardine, where the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) comes from, then it perambulates through half a dozen Liberal constituencies and finally winds up near where the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) comes from. Now, a body of men connected with this salt industry came before the tariff board and made the following application:
fMr. Kaiser.l
Application by the Salt Producers Association for cancellation of the item providing free salt for sea or gulf fishing; for increase of duty on salt imported in bags, barrels or other coverings or in bulk; for the imposition of the same rates of duty on containers filled with salt as applies on empty containers; and for increased duties on free-running table salt.
These business men in a business way put forward a business proposition. They did not complain that they were hard up, they did not say that their business was lagging. They simply said: We have a wonderful salt deposit in our section of the country, but we are hampered in our operations by salt coming in from the United States, from Germany and from the United Kingdom; we claim that if this salt were subject to a duty we would have the full advantage of our home market, we could operate to the full extent of our capacity and we could employ twice as many men. They did not say that they wanted to make more money, but they simply said they were working only 50 per cent cf their capacity. Then the notifying work began. In this houje there is something we see on the table, but there is also a game going on under the table that we do not see. When this matter came before this house all we know is that somebody got in contact with the Minister of Finance, with the result that the government said to the saJlt producers' association: We will grand a rebate of 99 per cent on the coal that you use in the preparation of your salt. That is the most ridiculous line that was ever written into a budget. I will tell you why. It illustrates the difference between the Conservative view and the Liberal view in handling such a mater. We say that the industry should be considered. Here is a means by which 500 families representing 2,500 people could be retained in Canada if the request for the imposition of a duty on salt were granted. But the Liberal mind says: We must fix up the industrialists; we will allow them every January to come down to parliament and by drawbacks take out of the cash box about $5,000 apiece. There are about ten factories engaged in the salt industry in western Ontario, and in the aggregate they turn out 200,000 tons of salt annually. It requires about
100,000	tons of coal to produce this salt. Fifty cents a ton on the coal means a drawback of about $50,000 which is divided up among these ten men. But they did not want it. They are sportsmen, and they take more pride in developing their industry than in getting a $5,000 drawback. That drawback did not add one solitary factory to our industrial development; it did not result in the employment of one additional workman. Two days ago the Canadian Salt Company issued their

The Budget-Mr. Kaiser
annual statement from their offices in Montreal, from which it appears that notwithstanding the fact that they have been able to operate only at half their capacity they earned 13i per cent on their capital. Before the tariff board it was shown that the salt manufacturers combined made 25 per cent on their capital. It was not a little drawback that they wanted. Like the good, honest, solid Canadians that I have always found in our industrial captains, they took far more pride in the development of their business and in the employment of fellow-Canadians than in securing the few paltry dollars offered thorn in drawbacks.

I can quite appreciate the fact that a drawback is justifiable and perfectly sound from a national point of view. If a man brings in ins raw material from a foreign country and manufactures it in Canada and then exports the finished product he is entitled to drawback. And the law permits it. But when it comes to giving drawbacks to some people in lieu of some other things they would like to have, it seems to me that this is absolutely wrong. What should this country do? Only one thing: the people should get rid of a government which fails to take advantage of the opportunities that offer; they want to do away with a job-killing government and replace it with a job-making administration. Read the remarks of the president of the Bank of Montreal a few days ago and you will get an idea of what should be the immigration policy of this country. From time immemorial people have moved from one country to another for one of two reasons;
cither to improve their position or to find employment. If this government only had sufficient faith in the country and could be induced to change its course and adopt a policy of protection, and provide that protection openly and honestly at the front door instead of at the back door, endeavouring thereby to provide employment for those people who are already in Canada as well as for others who might wish to come-if this were done we could dispense with a minister of immigration altogether.
The chief business before the country today is to undertake by every means possible to provide work for the people. Someone will ask, what about the automobile business in Oshawa? The government amended the tariff in this industry and I do not propose to say much on that score. The change was intended to effect great results. But what has happened? People generally do not realise it, but there has been an increase of 28 per cent in importations of automobiles into Canada, every one of which could have been manufactured in this country by Canadian workmen. This would have provided employment for 2,000 men. Reckoning five members to a family, this would mean 10,000 of a population who might have been retained in the country. But by one stroke of the pen the government drives from our shores all these people and then calls upon the Minister of Immigration to tour the world in search of
10,000	others to come in and take their place. The government, so to speak, are pouring material in at the top of the sack while it is running out at the bottom. If they only had sufficient common sense to sew up the hole at the bottom of the sack they would save all the loss that is now going on. The most pathetic thing I have ever witnessed was a village which was destroyed by tariff changes. Would any other country be guilty of such a thing? I venture to say you would not find the United States government following any course which would result in the shutting down of a single industry or the closing-up of a single home resulting in the exodus of its population. This sort of thing must come to an end in Canada. The government must have a change of heart or it will be the business of the people of this Dominion to put in a government who will see to it that sufficient work is provided for all.
On motion of Mr. Bennett the debate was adjourned.']

The Budget-Mr. Laflamme

The house resumed from Friday, March 9, consideration of the motion of Hon. J. A Robb (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Cahan and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Fansher (East Lambton).
Mr. LEO K. LAFLAMME (Montmagny) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, I had a notion of making use of the English language to express the few remarks that I wished to make to-day. However, when I think that there are still, in this house especially, hon. members who propound the fallacy of a one language country, I deemed it my duty to make use of my native tongue, in order to prove to them that we are really living in a bilingual country.
I do not presume at this stage of the debate, to put forth entirely new arguments or to be the first to discuss certain phases of the budget speech. However, I cannot let the opportunity slip by of congratulating the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), on his budget proposals, also the government on the present state of affairs, as the favourable financial statement of the country shows. On the whole, the great majority of Canadian people are satisfied with the situation such as it is. An outstanding proof of this, is the numerous speeches of our Conservative friends who attempt to destroy, by the multiplicity of incongruous and incoherent criticisms, often without foundation, the good effect of the present budget proposals. I may state that in my riding most of the people are satisfied, realizing that our government has made genuine efforts to remedy the difficult situation in which our opponents had left the country's finances, in 1921. Confidence again was restored the moment they heard that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), was announcing surpluses, for instance that of $42,000,000 for this year. The decrease of the national debt by $105,000,000, in the course of the last five years of the Liberal regime, is not of a nature to shatter the hopes of Canadians. Once more our people breathe easier. Realizing the enormity of a debt created not only by an exaggerated participation in the war, but by the wastefulness of public money, by a government caring little for the time-honoured interests of the people, Canadians now understand better the wisdom they showed in placing their hopes in the Liberal party. In the past, it was under the Liberal rule that the people

saw prosperity give rise to the hope of a brilliant century for Canada. To-day, they rejoice in seeing those who advocated a liberal policy for the masses, tackling a depressing financial situation, struggling courageously to solve the problem, while giving the greatest possible relief by decreasing the taxes.
According to our Conservative friends, the people are not justified! in placing their confidence in this administration. Everything is going wrong, they say. Yet, if we study the financial statements of the various institutions, we find that last year was a very prosperous one. I am going to quote from the Canadian Pacific's review "Agricultural and Industrial Progress in Canada" of February last:
The increasing ability of Canada to absorb her own bonds has been a feature of the past few years as the energetic efforts of the postwar period bore fruit in greater prosperity for the Dominion and its people. .
A little further on:
Canada has worked energetically and steadily to overcome the handicaps resulting from her participation in the war, and it is gratifying to note the reward of such effort. Youthful and with her wealth of resources barely tapped, Canada is a wealthy nation. Considering she has but finally emerged from the depression and, in the opinion of industrial and financial leaders is on the threshold of an era of unparalleled development, the future holds boundless possibilities for her and her people.
' But I think enough has been said to establish that Canada is on the road to the greatest prosperity ever experienced.
' Our opponents seem to nurse a grudge against the department of Immigration. Although they have only discovered the case of MtaCoruachie-a case deserving sympathy- they blame the hon. Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke), because all the efforts of the department were of no avail in keeping all the immigrants here, and stemming, at the same time, the emigration of our people. On this score-I have already had occasion of pointing it out-I see no necessity of bringing here more immigrants unless they are genuine settlers, capable of becoming true Canadians.
I fail to understand) why it is necessary to bring here young Englishmen and teach them to love farming.
First, very few of those born among the industrial classes, succeed on the farm. I rather think that something ought to foe done to encourage those of our people who, for one 'cause or another, wish to continue farming life somewhere outside their native province. By making grants to transportation companies who are more interested in numbers than in quality, we still persist in the error which strikes us to-day, in that connection: consider-

The Budget-Mr. Laflamme
able sums are spent and we do not rea.p the benefit expected. First and above all, let us give Canadians the same facilities as we give to foreigners.
1 Rural credit is certainly called upon to render appreciable services to the farming class. We already have, in the province of Quebec, an admirable institution: the "Caisses populaires " (people's savings banks)-which I would like to see better understood and more numerous-which have rendered and are still rendering great services to our farmers.
There is also our educational system which, especially in the business colleges, does not lend itself sufficiently to the training of young people for the farm. We have noted this deficiency and the harm wrought, and we are trying to remedy it. All depends on this: teach the young men to cultivate a taste for the land because it is the principal wealth, the national domain, pre-eminently; endeavour to have then understand its primary usefulness; impress on them what better returns they may have from the land, by having recourse to better methods. That is the ideal towards which our educational system should tend.
How many times have I noted the benefit derived from the putting into practice of the modem teachings on agriculture? The success of one would make the hesitation of others fade away and, by the means of examples, in a few years we would be astonished to see the improvement which has taken place. Speaking more especially in behalf of my district, I would ask the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), not to discontinue the services of the Seed Control Board, at Quebec. Our farmers have already greatly benefited from it. If they are somewhat backward in taking advantage of these services, we must not forget that we should proceed slowly in the propaganda of modem methods of farming, if we wish their success.
I can but congratulate the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) and his department, which encourages sheep raising by granting subsidies.
The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence), was rather in a humorous mood the other day, and seemed to be sympathetic as to the lot of the Quebec farmers, which was in contrast to certain statements made previous to the Winnipeg convention, last autumn. He said:
But under the Australian treaty the business is suffering so seriously that it will not be long now before the only thing we shall have to eat will be Australian mutton. We shall not be able to produce a lamb chop in Canada; that will be a luxury reserved entirely for the millionaire.
I might tell the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) that, thanks to the assistance given by the department of Agriculture, our people in Quebec have understood the advantage there was for them to take up sheep raising, and that in my county, the four central parishes-Notre-Dame-du-Rosaire especially-made a start, not very long ago, in raising sheep; last year their sheep were graded as first quality on the Montreal market. They will not rest satisfied even at that, this year we shall have a finer and larger number of sheep.
To help to increase our population and keep our people in this country, the governments- federal and provincial

must unite in a strenuous educational campaign. They will soon notice that the money thus spent is not a loss, and with the same assistance granted to Canadian settlers, special personal transportation rates and free grants of land as well as pecuniary or farming assistance during the first years, the problem will have soon lost of its magnitude.
I see no necessity of accepting the suggestions prompted by our interested and distinguished visitors-among others the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs-who seems to want to direct our course in immigration matters. Our authorities are sufficiently well posted to know what should be done to solve our problems. As for us, we have not the boldness to suggest a solution to the problems which these visitors have themselves in their own country.
Our opponents have done much talking about ruin, unemployment, closed mills and further works stopping after the budget was put into force. Unemployment is far more felt in other countries than it is among us, and to give weight to what the hon. members on this side of the house have said in regard to the United States, we have the statement of the Prime Minister of England, made in the House of Commons, on February 13, last: that there were a million unemployed in England. It is true, that in the town of Monbmagny, within my riding, the doors of a large plant have been closed since a few years, but I have no fear of stating that it is not because we have had no protection. It would be desirable that its doors opened again, and if the government-not by raising the tariff-could help us, we should feel very thankful. There are others which are prosperous, esepecially since the Liberal party is in power. The fears of a certain manufacturer that the coming into power of the Liberals would mean the closing of his factory

The Budget-Mr. Lafl.am.me
doors have been changed into unbounded hopes, since in 1927 he enlarged his plant and intends to further extend it this year.
Again referring to the criticisms of the Conservatives: according to statistics, the dairy industry has increased in 1927. Milk production amounted to 13,407,340,237 pounds against 12,651,388,490 pounds in 1926. Moreover the amount of cream amounted to 4,148,469,498 pounds and that of butter 2,223,950,000 pounds. Our best market is the United States. Still quoting the Canadian Pacific's review on this matter, we find that the' statements of our opponents do not coincide with actual facts:
So far from anything being wrong with the Canadian dairy industry, it is in sound shape, being worth, according to estimate, $250,000,000 per year, which makes it one of the most valuable branches of Canadian agriculture. The existing situation and that forecast justify considerable expansion, and that Canadian dairymen are awakening to the opportunity is frequently made apparent. The number of cows on farms in Canada in 1927 showed a gratifying increase, while the Dominions recently produced a new world champion producer in butter fat. Both Ontario and Quebec dairymen have formed associations the better to engage in the shipment of milk and cream to the United States. There is unquestionably a profitable future ahead for those engaging or coming to engage in dairy production in Canada.
They bitterly complained that our favourable balance of trade had decreased in 1927. If it is but $131,218,843 this year, there is no cause for alarm. Quoting again, from the same source, we find the explanation:
The reduction in this balance occasions no uneasiness, but on the contrary is accepted as a healthy sign since it is stated to be accountable to the great increase in construction in Canada. The purchase of machinery and construction material has swelled imports, while many people have been engaged in building construction who would otherwise be producing goods for export.
Like the hon. member for Beauhamois (Mr. Raymond) did, I wish to draw the attention of the hon. minister for Defence (Mr. Ralston), to the proposed estimates of his department. No doubt, we must adopt modem means, such as aviation, but let us not increase our expenditure as regards to armament, when other countries speak of disarmament and when England reduces its estimates in that respect, let us not increase our estimates to make up for England's deficiency on that score. If we have too much money, let us think of Quebec. Our province has not had its due share in railways.
As to the income tax, I think that we cannot possibly dispense with it now. We have to pay off a large debt and everybody has to contribute. Personally, I am in favour of increasing the limit of exemption so that

those who have large incomes will pay their share. Everybody must understand his responsibilities. The farmer more than any has felt the depreciation in values after the war, he was the first to accept the accomplished fact. Industries were longer in doing so; sooner or later they will have to accept it. In the meantime industries must help more than any other in carrying our burdens. I am not opposed to the legitimate and even substantial profits of enterprises, but again we must be fair and not have the consumer, after all, pay what the income tax collects from them on their profits.
I entirely approve of what has been said by the hon. member for Beauhamois (Mr. Raymond), and the hon. member for Hoche-laga (Mr. St-Pere), in regard to the income tax of corporations, especially those which sell electricity. On that score in my own town of Montmagny, the Quebec Power obliges us to pay 8 cents per K.W.H. for the lighting service. Everybody knows the enormous profits of these companies, and I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), for not having granted their request this year. I am somewhat astonished to read, in the Montreal Herald of March 9, the following warning:
We warn the government that there is a rising tide of indignation in the province of Quebec against this discrimination. Quebec is willing, and always has been willing, to contribute its fair share to the general expenses of the Dominion, but it will not calmly submit to being imposed upon.

speechtext: They know nothing about it.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not believe that this warning expresses really the popular feeling of the province of Quebec.

speechtext: I must object to that. The guarantees of the Minister of Finance in regard to the Canadian National Railways are shown in the public accounts; they are schedule 5 of the balance sheet. My hon. friend, in attributing the statement he did to me, was not distinguishing between the terms net debt and public accounts.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps I inadvertently used the term public accounts. As a matter of fact, if the money is advanced in cash to the railway by the Minister of Finance, it appears in the ordinary balance sheet of the Dominion, but if it is provided by way of guarantees, it appears only in the accounts of the Canadian National Railways.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No. It appears in a
schedule of the balance sheet, in the public accounts of Canada.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It does not appear as part of the net debt of the Dominion itself.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is right.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In other words, if this amount of approximately $50,000,000 which was guaranteed by the Minister of Finance last year for t!he Canadian National Railways, had been advanced in cash to the railway, then the whole surplus claimed by the hon. Minister of Finance, and more, would have disappeared during the past year. And yet the gross liabilities of this Dominion, direct and indirect are exactly the same in either case. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, whether under this system of keeping the accounts it is not possible that some Finance minister some day may be tempted to put out misleading statements? In other words, the Minister of Finance has it in his own hands either to advance the cash for the requirements of the Canadian National Railways, which would appear in the net debt of the Dominion, or to guarantee the bonds of the Canadian National Railways, which would not appear in the net debt of the Dominion. I can imagine some Minister of Finance saying in the middle of the year, along in September, when it is usually necessary to raise some money for the purpose of financing, "Shall I provide this money in cash out of the coffers of the Dominion exchequer, or shall I guar-



The Budget-Sir George Perley
antee the bonds of the Canadian National Railways? If I provide this money in cash out of the Dominion exchequer, I am going to have to show a deficit next year in my budget speech, but if I provide it by guarantees, then I shall be able to show a surplus in my next budget speech." I claim and submit, Mr. Speaker, that irrespective of party this question of keeping the accounts should be straightened out and put in proper shape. The accounts should be kept just as would be done in the case of any large corporation in this country. I know it is argued that the system here is followed by other governments in this country, but to my mind that does not make it right.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And by my hon. friend's government.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I expected that. We always get the tu quoque argument. But we on this side of the house are always trying to learn something, while hon. gentlemen opposite do not seem to wish to learn.
Now a few words with regard to the argument put forward the other day by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). I was rather surprised to find a gentleman of his ability and capacity making use of that old campaign trick with which we are all familiar, of putting up a dummy and then knocking it down. When we first go into a campaign, probably we all use that trick, but as we get older we often find that it is wiser to drop it. At page 1055 of Hansard the hon. Minister of Justice says:
I was hoping that he (the leader of the opposition) would discountenance his followers in their campaign of belittling and misrepresenting Canada in the eyes of the world. Why glorify the United States at the expense of Canada ?	-
The hon. gentleman knows as well as I do there is no foundation for any suggestion of that kind. What right has the hon. Minister of Justice to say or even to suggest that we on this side are belittling Canada? That is an argument which is used in this country at elections, but it seems to me it might well be dropped. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, I ask anyone who will answer in a conscientious way, whether there are any more loyal Canadians than we who sit on the left of Your Honour. I for one am proud of Canada, and proud of what we have accomplished in this country. I lived in England for eight years, in a very responsible position. I had an interesting time and a great deal of work to do, and I was glad to do anything I could during those war years, but my wife and I always looked forward to the day. when we might come back to our old home, and as soon as the opportunity

offered we came back here, because we think this is the best country in the world1 in which we can live, and I certainly do not like the Minister of Justice to suggest anything different.
We on this side of the house, Mr. Speaker, are rather tired of having the government relying upon Providence alone for the blessings this country enjoys. It seems to us that it is high time the government did something to try and make Canada an even better country to live in; that they tried to make use of the raw materials and opportunities for development in this country, to give more work for our Canadian boys and girls, and to increase our population. I for one do not like the present conditions under which we are spending money to teach our boys and girls in our schools, and then to have them find no opportunity for their talents here, and leave this country and go elsewhere to make a living. They are our best raw material and we ought to do everything we possibly can to keep them here, and to make as much work and provide as many opportunities for them as possible, and I suggest to the government that they get busy and make a real effort to provide more work for our people at home, both on the farms and in the factories. Instead of taking this view of the case, the Minister of Justice prefers, as I judge from what he says, although I hope I am wrong, to ship out our raw material, and he apparently glories in that fact because I find on page 1056 of Hansard, the following extract which he read from some publication:
The total per capita exports of all lines from the United States is $39.62, from Canada, $122.57.
He glories in that fact; he boasts of it. I take the other view. Our exports are largely of raw materials, whereas United States exports of raw materials are less in proportion to population. Why? Because they use them up in their own country, thus providing work for their own people. Therefore, rather than glory in the fact that we export more raw materials than the United States do in proportion to population, the government should endeavour to stop some of this exportation of raw material and have it made into more highly finished products, thus keeping at home many of our young people who are now going away.
I humbly submit that the government should consider adopting the plan that we on this side of the house advocate of making our laws in such a way that we shall manufacture in this country everything we can instead of buying it largely from the United States. It is not fair that in our competition

The Budget-Sir George Perley
with our friends across the line, because they are and I am sure they always will be friends of ours, we should be handicapped by their very heavy tariff and at the same time by the fact that under our lower tariff they are able to ship goods into this country while we cannot ship goods into theirs. In this connection I wish particularly to refer to the farmers and fruit growers. I spoke of this at a previous session and I feel very strongly on the point. I believe the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) thinks as I do that this home market of ours should be kept as much as possible for our own home growers. The purpose of the Conservative policy, as I take it, to encourage our industries is twofold. One idea is to provide more work for the people in our factories and the other is to provide in our own country a greater market for our farmers and fruit growers. My constituency is an agricultural one with several industries which keep up the towns, and in that way the people who live in the towns are first-class customers at good prices for the products of the farms round about. I need hardly say to you, Mr. Speaker-and everybody will agree in this-that whatever we grow in this country is the best that grows anywhere. It matters not whether we talk about apples, potatoes or people-they are the best that are grown anywhere and able to stand up against competition in any part of the world. But is it just that farmers and fruit growers in this northern climate should be subjected to unfair competition from southern countries where it costs less to produce these articles?
Under the present tariff laws in the United States the president or some committee has power to increase the duties when necessity warrants. I have known cases of this kind where some Canadians have worked up an export market in the United States. A very glaring one that occurred last year was that of a clothing manufacturer in Toronto. They had worked up a market in Detroit even under the high tariff but they found that they could make the business pay. This was discovered by customs officials in the United States and a shipment which was sent out on an order from the Toronto house to Detroit was stopped at the border and the tariff was raised before the shipment could be delivered. We should not submit to treatment such as that.

speechtext: They can impose an embargo if they see fit.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend
tells me that they could put on an embargo if they saw fit. I am not one of those who 56103-761
advocate a sky-high tariff, but in this trade competition 'between us and our friends and neighbours to the south, I think it is the duty of this parliament and this government to give our people as much opportunity as possible to do business and to earn their living.
The following incident is a small matter but these little things show how the wind blows. This is an extract from the Ottawa Citizen of Friday or Saturday last:
Pickles and sauces served on the tables in the parliamentary restaurant in the House of Commons were yesterday found by a delegation from the Canadian Horticultural Council to be manufactured in the United States. The delegation waited on government authorities and brought this fact to their attention, with the request that the government "practise what it preaches"-use goods made in Canada. Both pickles and sauces are manufactured in Canada.
Could anything be more ludicrous than that we should use in our own parliamentary restaurant pickles and sauces made in the United States?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I suggest one thing more ludicrous-protectionists wearing Italian felt hats.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I take it that my hon. friend is in favour of the produce of the farms of this country being used here as much as possible. He will agree with me in that, at all events. The government may say: Oh, that is a matter for the committee- that administers the restaurant. But as a matter of fact the government supporters control that committee; they are in a majority on the1 committee on the restaurant, and if they gave instructions that there were to be no more of these articles used unless they were made in Canada, their orders would be carried out.
I lived at the Chateau Laurier for several years and canned fruit is something I use a good deal of. I did not have many things to grumble' about at the Chateau Laurier, but I certainly did complain because I could not get from them any peaches except United States peaches. We raise in this country better peaches than they do in California or Oregon, and why the Canadian National Railways should supply what is really a government hotel with fruit from across the line when we have better fruit in Canada, is something I have always failed to understand. In other words I take the ground that particularly in regard to the products of the farm and the competition with farmers and fruit growers in the United States, steps should be taken to protect our growers in order that they may have their home market for themselves when they are denied an opportunity to sell their produce across the line. The Department of

The Budget-Sir George Perley
Agriculture of this government has quite properly urged a campaign for the use of Canadian products. Why do they not do it themselves? Surely they should be the first to set us an example. We vote $30,000 a year to run the parliamentary restaurant. I have not ascertained if all the appropriation was used last year. But surely the government, and especially my friend the Minister of Agriculture, who goes up and down the country urging on the people the wisdom- with which I agree-of using Canadian products, might at least practise what they preach.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, until this morning I had hoped to keep out of this already too long-drawn-out debate, but when I learned that I could have a period of forty minutes or less without prolonging the debate in the aggregate, I thought I would take advantage of it.
So far as the budget proper is concerned, with the naked eye I cannot see that any indentations have been made in it during the three weeks it has been under bombardment. I think the budget is just as popular throughout the country to-day as when it was first laundhed. Then why deal with it any further?
Before considering a number of the statements on immigration and dairying that have been made in the course of this debate, let me refer to the concluding remarks of the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) who has just resumed his seat. Pickles and sauces! A serious matter indeed,-if 't were true. But I am sorry to tell my hon. friend that the statement is not true, according to what Mr. George tells me. He was in my office the other day and expressed great concern about the impression that had been created that pickles made in the United States were being served in the parliamentary restaurant. He assured me that this is not the case.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am glad to hear it.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sorry to spoil my hon. friend's little story. He and his friends must be in a pretty bad pickle when they have to resort ito such criticism. I am afraid I may have to spoil some more of their little stories and castles in the air before I am through.
Now then, as to immigration. This, I admit, is a very important question. Apparently one of the chief complaints has been made by my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Quinn), and reiterated by twenty or thirty of his associates. It concerns a certain family that was detained at Halifax, with the result that two
*Sir George Perley.]
of its members were not allowed to land. But there is a much larger question at stake than the hardship entailed on this individual family. Shall we keep out the prohibited classes, or shall we let them in? There are something like twenty-five or thirty prohibited classes mentioned in section 3 of the Immigration Act-imbeciles, the feebleminded, idiots, epileptics, prostitutes and pimps-whatever those are; these are all prohibited. Now, if I understand the complaints against the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke), some at least of these prohibited classes should have been let in, and the treatment of the McConachie family has raised the question. But, as I say, a much larger question is involved. Why should these prohibited classes be allowed to enter the Dominion? I do not care whether the law prohibits their entry or not, or even if the Minister of Immigration has discretion, to let them in,-did he not do the right thing in keeping this class of people out? While I was a provincial minister, acting in the Department of Labour and in the Department of Health, I had to deport a considerable number of immigrants from Saskatchewan. I found after sifting them down as closely as possible that some of the no-goods gain entry once in a while, and they have to be deported. Then why deliberately permit these prohibited classes to come in?-the classes that I have described. There is a big issue at stake. If I interpret correctly the position taken by my hon. friend from Halifax and other hon. members of the opposition, they are asking that the two members of the McConachie family-one prohibited-to whom I have referred should have been allowed to land. If we are to allow the simple-minded to come in then what about the idiots, the imbeciles, the epileptics, and the others specified in section 3-fifteen or twenty prohibited classes? If one is allowed to enter, why not two; and if two, why not a thousand? If you allow one of the prohibited classes to come in, the whole twenty classes can come in. There we take issue with our friends on the other side. We feel sorry for these unfortunates, but, nevertheless, we believe that, as in the past, they should be kept out. There can be no compromise on this question.

In 1922 it was 45 cents. Parenthetically I would point out that changes in freight rates downwards, due to some specific policy or

action on the part of this government, have been invariably opposed by hon. gentlemen opposite. In September 1922, for some reason that does not appear on the face of it, the rate, was increased to 49 cents, but in January, 1924, it was reduced to 43 cents; and in September, 1925, it was further reduced to 354 cents. This meant a total reduction in the rate from Grande Prairie to Fort William per hundred pounds during that period of 244 cents. Let us take the freight rate from Grande Prairie to Vancouver during the same period. In 1921 it was 54 cents; in 1922, 48 cents; in 1923, 43 cents; on January 19, 1924, 404 cents; on January 29, 1924, 394 cents and in September, 1925, 294 cents; while on September 15, 1925, it was 28 cents. This represents a total reduction per hundred pounds from Grande Prairie to Vancouver of 304 cents; in other words, the rate was more than cut in two. That would permit the farmers of Grande Prairie to carry on while the country was developing and tonnage improving in order to warrant an outlet to the Pacific. We believe that two things must run concurrently; we must prepare for an outlet to the Pacific, which undoubtedly will come; and simultaneously with that preparation we as a government must make it possible for the farmers there to carry on with a reasonable profit on their efforts. And this is the best means towards that end. We must reduce freight rates to that extent and thus reduce the cost of production of every bushel of grain. I may say that settlement is taking place rapidly there, and not settlement of the feeble-minded either, but of strong, sturdy vigorous men and women. These people are going into that country and making it the envy of the whole continent. Herman Trel'le went there as a young man, an engineer, and going in for farming he was able eventually to capture first prizes on the continent in both wheat and oats. He did this two years ago, and where did he get his wheat? He got it from the experimental farm in Ottawa. I am ready to give him all the time he desires for the purpose. In the meantime, that is all we can do and we shall pass on to something else.
Our friends have taken umbrage at the Australian treaty. Well, of course, you cannot buy a market without paying for it; somebody has to pay. When the British preference was first established in 1897 it could not be done without somebody's toes being hurt a little. But in the main it was good for Canada. In the main the Australian treaty is good for Canada, and we hope it is good for Australia as well. This government, led by the Prime Minister, are strongly in favour of developing interimperial trade, as I am sure we all are, and you cannot do that except at an occasional cost to some one. You would almost think, Mr. Speaker, that it was actually a crime to eat good Australian or New Zealand butter; apparently our hon. friends would rather have the people of Canada eating oleomargarine. I remember one of the first remarks I ever made in this house; it was not from this seat, but from somewhere in this vicinity, and it had to do with this question of oleomargarine. My hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton), whom we are glad to see back in his seat looking well and happy, was very much entertained by the discussion which then took place, and he can probably recall it quite well.

I have a list of the importations from the Antipodes for the last twenty years, and during every year we have had occasion to import more or less Antipodean butter into Canada to eke out our own supply during the winter months. Is that a crime? During the last year of the Liberal administration, in 1911, 903,821 pounds of butter were imported, while during the first year of the Conservative administration in 1912 the figure jumped to 2,241,584 pounds. I am not going to blame them for that; if they had no butter for their bread they did well to get it wherever they could, and they were so anxious to get it that they supplemented the butter with oleomargarine. Then in 1913 the importation jumped to 6,116,134 pounds; in 1914 it amounted to 6,959,757 pounds, and this country seemed to survive all right. That has gone on year by year. For the first ten months of this year we imported 8,228,986 pounds of butter, and I anticipate that before the year is over the figure will be even larger. Where is the crime in that? The funny part of it is that our friends opposite are pleading largely on behalf of the urban population of this country; they tell us they are getting butter too cheaply.
I can understand the objection of the farmers to the Australian treaty, but I cannot understand the urban people objecting to good Australian butter at about two cents less per pound. As I have said, I can well understand the objection of the farmer, but to judge the relative policies of the two parties on this one issue you must not take any isolated item; you must deal with the whole policy of the government. Therefore, when you size up the policy of our friends opposite, you must consider that policy not only in relation to the importation of butter but also in regard to the free importation of oleomargarine and its ingredients. Imagine Tories letting anything in free! However, they were partial to this concoction of intestinal fats and southern oils which was called oleomargarine, and the ingredients were allowed in free. Then you must also remember that when the treaty with the West Indies was negotiated, Canada received a specific preference of one and one-half cents per pound on butter. Consequently, when you consider the policies of the two parties, you must agree that our policy is infinitely preferable to the one inaugurated by our predecessors. I do not suppose my hon. friends want any more of these figures, so I will say nothing more than that during every one of the past twenty years more or less Australian butter came into Canada, and no one thinks it is a crime. As a matter of fact, in this treaty there is a provision by which, upon six months' notice, either party may amend or abrogate it, so it is not a fixture from now to eternity. It does not seem to be doing the urban people any harm, whatever effect it may have on our rural population.
Now I would like to refer to some matters on which the leader of the opposition touched in his initial speech, which was a very good one. I will not quote him, but he was in no better humour than were his followers. He did go so far as to admit that there was a certain amount of temporary prosperity in the country, but he did not like the way that prosperity was obtained. He did not like

the great mining development, for instance, because it was so hard on the mines; he did not like the development in our pulp and paper industry because it was so hard on the forests, and he did not like the big crops, apparently, because they were so hard on the land. He might have said with greater truth that he did not like the result of the last election, because it was so hard on the Tories. I remember the time he went down to Portage la Prairie to help out his late lamented leader, and instead of helping him he drove home the last nail in the lid of the coffin of that leader, which has not been raised since.
